בְּהֹנוֹת יָדָיו rendered by the single word thumbs, which carries both morphemes' senses, English writing thumbs of hands only as it writes great toes of feet only; the two lexical nouns share one unit headed on the morpheme carrying the lexeme (rule 30, as with דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים -> chronicles). The suffix keeps its own his under rule 18.
The gapped thumbs-of clause is rendered great toes; the noun takes the whole expression, headed on toes (rule 31).

review_notes: Corrected: יָדָיו had been marked unrepresented under rule 22 with the note that the ASV renders no word for hands. Rule 22's first sentence governs an element the ASV has left unwritten, and its closing paragraph directs that one ask first whether the English word carries the morpheme's sense; thumbs does, since English writes it of hands only, which is the very contrast the ASV draws with great toes in the next colon. The pair is now one rule 30 unit headed on בְּהֹנוֹת.
יָד is not a repeated or resumptive element in any case: what the Hebrew repeats and then gaps is בֹּהֶן, in the feet colon, so rule 22 never reached this token.

The competing reading leaves יָד unrepresented. It was rejected because rule 30 forbids leaving one member of such a pair unrepresented beside a neighbour holding the whole rendering, and because rule 40's בֶּאֱמֶת -> faithfully sentence rejects the objection that thumbs is merely בֹּהֶן's ordinary rendering: what decides it is that a single English word stands for the pair.
great toes is still given whole to רַגְלָיו, whose own בֹּהֶן the Hebrew gaps, headed on toes; the alternative heads it on great.
